native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Incarceration is associated with a substantially lower and slower-growing wealth trajectory for Black respondents, with the penalty concentrated among those starting from the HIGHEST baseline wealth/income-status. Because no income/earnings variable exists, 'income level' was proxied by baseline composite_wealth_1985 (a wealth/income-status stock proxy), split into a zero/negative group plus four quartiles of positive baseline wealth. In every stratum, ever-jailed Black respondents held less wealth than non-jailed peers in 1996, and in the two highest wealth tiers the jailed group actually LOST wealth between 1990 and 1996 (e.g., 'High' tier jailed: $53,538 in 1990 → $9,590 in 1996, vs. $53,538 → $80,741 for non-jailed). A difference-in-differences contrast over the cleaner post-incarceration window (1990→1996) shows a negative jailed-minus-non-jailed wealth change in all tiers (−$11,500 in the zero/negative tier to −$98,682 in the 'High' tier), and over the full 1985→1996 span the associated wealth gap GROWS monotonically with baseline wealth tier (−$17,483 → −$28,510 → −$37,864 → −$71,384 → −$48,583). A regression of 1996 wealth on ever_jailed with baseline-wealth-tier interactions confirms a strong negative main effect (≈ −$20,000 for the lowest tier, p<0.01) that becomes progressively larger in the higher tiers (≈ −$54,000 to −$55,000 for the 'High' and 'Top' tiers, both p<0.001). Thus, among Black respondents, being ever jailed is associationally linked to a steeper wealth penalty the higher one's starting wealth/income-status, with the largest absolute losses—and a reversal from accumulation to dis-accumulation—at the top of the distribution. This is an associational finding, not causal: income is proxied by baseline wealth, ever_jailed is an indirect/self-reported incarceration proxy, per-tier jailed cells are small (18-76), and the jail window (1985-1994) overlaps the 1985 baseline so the 1990→1996 post-period contrast is the primary trajectory comparison.
native_result.WorkflowB: Restricted to race=='black' (N=3,013; 159 jailed, 5.28%, 143 male). Built income/wealth-status tiers from baseline composite_wealth_1985 (explicit zero/negative group + quartiles of positive baseline wealth at $1,800/$5,300/$14,337). Computed (A) mean 1985/1990/1996 wealth by tier x ever_jailed; (B) difference-in-differences (jailed minus non-jailed change) over the primary 1990→1996 post window and the full 1985→1996 span per tier with Welch t-tests; (C) OLS regressions (HC1 robust SEs) of 1996 wealth on ever_jailed + baseline wealth + sex + tier dummies, then + ever_jailed x tier interactions, plus a log(1+wealth) robustness model and a 1990→1996 post-change outcome model. Framed associational, not causal. Executed script: analysis.py; full output: analysis_output.txt.
